summary: Budget week: Champagne pitches a plan to lift productivity, Trump says a trade deal is "very close", factories shrink, and Ontario probes alleged OSAP fraud.
body: Thursday's federal budget is two days away. On Monday, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told a Toronto business audience it is about "changing Canada's growth model": getting companies to invest more so workers produce more. He hinted at tax breaks for small businesses but gave no dollar figures [^3]. The Parliamentary Budget Officer expects a $63.3-billion deficit this year, smaller than it forecast in June [^1]. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wants federal diesel taxes and the GST on fuel paused and spending cut [^1].

Trade talks with the US may be moving. Prime Minister Mark Carney and President Trump spoke on Saturday (not Sunday, as yesterday's brief said), and Trump now says the two countries are "very close" to a deal [^2]. Carney says the US has been "coming closer" to Canada's position, but asked whether Trump would sign, he said "I don't know that" [^2]. No terms are public. Carney is at the Commonwealth leaders' meeting in Antigua and Barbuda this week [^6].

The tariffs are showing up in factories. A monthly survey of manufacturers fell to 49.6 in October; below 50 means the sector is shrinking, the first time this year. New orders dropped, and costs rose at the fastest pace in over four years [^4].

For students: Ontario alleges in court documents that one internet address sent more than half of the OSAP student-aid applications at two campuses of a private career college. The claims are unproven, and the school denies wrongdoing [^5]. The province has paused payments to all private post-secondary schools, called in the OPP and ordered an audit; opposition critics ask why this was missed while OSAP grants for public college and university students were cut this year [^5]. My read: Thursday's budget and any trade deal matter most for jobs this winter.
differences: The government says the budget answers a time of "profound change and uncertainty"; Poilievre says it should cut spending and fuel taxes [^1]. The PBO expects Ottawa to miss its own goal of a falling deficit-to-GDP ratio [^1]. On trade, Trump says a deal is "very close", Carney says he does not know if Trump will sign, and Poilievre says Carney broke his promise of a better deal [^2].
